newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Ecu vulnerable, core Europe preferred.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Ecu vulnerable, core Europe preferred.

text.p: Ecu bonds are vulnerable while concerns about a delay to the start of European Economic and Monetary Union remain, and investors should consider core Europe as a safe haven, analysts said on Monday.
European economic and finance ministers are meeting in Brussels on Monday to discuss preparations for EMU, but this is not expected to throw any further light on the possible delay.
"We probably won't get too much clarity after the meeting," said James Mitchell, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"What is important in deciding whether EMU is going to happen on time or not is whether Germany can meet the three percent (deficit to GDP) criteria," he said.
Analysts said the key event would be the meeting of the German tax committee in early May when the fiscal deficit forecast would be set for the rest of the year.

"Once we see those estimates we will see the exact extent of the hole in the budget and the government will then have an opportunity to plug it," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International in London.
He said once the German government's reaction was known and if EMU looked more likely, some stability should come back into the market.
At 1148 GMT, the 10-year Ecu/Bund yield spread was at 47 basis points, compared with 29 basis points in early January.
Brickman said the gap had widened on the back of the underperformance of Italy and Spain.
"While those countries remain vulnerable, the Ecu itself remains vulnerable," he said. "Confidence is not going to come back into the Ecu until you get confidence in the constituent parts."
He said for now, the safety play for investors was Germany with other members of core Europe, like the Netherlands and Belgium, also offering relatively good security.
Longer term, Mitchell said the high yielding markets would also be attractive.

"Obviously at the moment people are panicking a bit...you don't really want to jump in at these levels," he said. "But after the mini budget Italy should get its deficit down to three percent and bonds will probably look as good as Germany, if not better." Italy is due to present its mini budget by the end of April.
Some analysts were more positive for Ecu bonds, seeing the recent underperformance as offering a good buying opportunity.

Mary Bloom, Ecu/EMU bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said comments from German finance minister Theo Waigel over the weekend had damaged high yielders more than the ECU market. Waigel said fulfilling the EMU criteria was more important than sticking to a strict timetable.

"The Ecu market so far is holding up fairly well, it has been relatively quiet this morning and is showing signs of normal Monday morning conditions," she said. "It is not underperforming as much as the high yielding markets."
There was a lot of talk and a lot of speculation over EMU, she said, but few actual strategies had been put into place as far as the Ecu market was concerned.

"In theory a delay in EMU would be bad for Ecu assets but from the way the Ecu bond market is behaving one can see that investors are not putting big money onto a delay scenario yet," Bloem said. "Our base scenario is that there is still a majority chance for EMU to go ahead on time, with a limited number of European countries."
"With this in mind, we feel this underperforming of the Ecu market is definitely a buying opportunity. In particular we favour the six to eight year sector," she said.
